summarySteps: 1. CRR Step Factors ([fact-01]): Up and down factors $u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}$ and $d = 1/u$ with risk-neutral probability $p = (a-d)/(u-d)$.
2. American Backward Induction ([fact-02]): Evaluates node values as $V = \max(	ext{Intrinsic}, e^{-r\Delta t}[p V_{up} + (1-p)V_{down}])$.
3. Control Variates ([fact-04]): Pairs tree pricing with European BSM analytical formulas to eliminate known discretization errors ($f_A = f_{	ext{tree}} + [f_{	ext{BSM}} - f_{	ext{tree}}]$).
4. Escrow Dividend Decomposition ([fact-05]): Decomposes stock into $S^* = S - D \cdot e^{-r t_D}$ to preserve recombining lattice efficiency ($N(N+1)/2$).
5. Monte Carlo Simulation ([fact-06]): Generates discrete risk-neutral Brownian motion paths via $S(t+\Delta t) = S(t)\exp[(r-q-0.5\sigma^2)\Delta t + \sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\epsilon]$.
6. Standard Error Scaling ([fact-07]): Standard error scales as $SE = \omega / \sqrt{M}$, requiring quadrupling paths ($4M$) to halve estimation error.
7. Method Comparative Strengths ([fact-08]): Binomial trees excel at American early exercise; Monte Carlo excels at path-dependent multi-asset exotics.
8. Institutional Calibration ([fact-10]): Standard trading desks use 50 to 100 steps paired with control variates for sub-second precision.
bottomTakeaway: Numerical procedures like Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binomial trees and Monte Carlo simulation provide robust institutional pricing frameworks, balancing American early exercise backward induction against path-dependent exotic simulation ([fact-02], [fact-04], [fact-06], [fact-08]).
